tts: How did a garden hose turn into a three-billion-franc shoe brand? To get it, let's go back to the very first sneakers.
In eighteen thirty-nine, Charles Goodyear figured out how to vulcanize rubber. Rubber soles were so quiet, you could sneak up on people. That's how sneakers got their name.
In nineteen thirty-six, Jesse Owens won four gold medals in spikes made by the Dassler brothers. Then the brothers fell out and started two rivals: Adidas and Puma.
In nineteen seventy-one, coach Bill Bowerman poured urethane into his wife's waffle iron. That waffle sole became one of Nike's first big hits.
In the late two-thousands, Swiss triathlete Olivier Bernhard cut up a garden hose and glued the pieces to a running shoe. Landing felt soft, and the push-off felt springy.
In twenty ten, he and two friends founded a company called On, in Zurich. The hose pieces became patented clouds.
In twenty nineteen, Roger Federer invested. And in twenty twenty-one, On went public in New York, valued at over eleven billion dollars.
Last year, sales jumped thirty percent, past three billion Swiss francs. Not bad for a piece of garden hose.
